claim: Stress-related disorders rank among the leading causes for disease burden world-wide.
source: Stress-related disorders rank among the leading causes for disease burden world-wide (GBD 2015 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to GBD 2015 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2016

claim: The global stress load has increased dramatically in recent years.
source: the global stress load has increased even more dramatically in recent years (Brooks et al., 2020; Robillard et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2020 and Robillard et al., 2020

claim: Contemplative mental training programs can be efficient in stress reduction.
source: research has shown that contemplative mental training programs can be efficient in stress reduction (Puhlmann et al., 2021b; Engert et al., 2023; Engert et al., 2017; for a meta-analysis see Khoury et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Puhlmann et al., 2021b; Engert et al., 2023; Engert et al., 2017; and a meta-analysis by Khoury et al., 2015

claim: Contemplative mental training programs can induce brain plasticity.
source: research has shown that contemplative mental training programs can be efficient in stress reduction (Puhlmann et al., 2021b; Engert et al., 2023; Engert et al., 2017; for a meta-analysis see Khoury et al., 2015), while simultaneously inducing brain plasticity (Valk et al., 2017; Pernet et al., 2021; Davidson, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Valk et al., 2017; Pernet et al., 2021; Davidson, 2016

claim: It is unclear which types of mental practices are most efficient in reducing stress and inducing stress-related brain plasticity.
source: It is, however, still unclear which types of mental practices are most efficient in reducing stress and inducing stress-related brain plasticity.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the literature

claim: Diurnal cortisol is a less investigated marker in the stress reduction context through contemplative mental training.
source: A less investigated marker in the stress reduction context through contemplative mental training is diurnal cortisol, from which summary indices such as the cortisol awakening response (CAR), the total diurnal output and the diurnal cortisol slope are frequently investigated (Ross et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about research gap, with citation to Ross et al., 2014 for cortisol indices

claim: Cortisol is the end-product of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis.
source: The steroid hormone and glucocorticoid cortisol is the end-product of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and a key player in stress regulation (for reviews see e.g., Chrousos, 2009; Sapolsky, 2000a).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by review citations to Chrousos, 2009 and Sapolsky, 2000a

claim: Cortisol is a key player in stress regulation.
source: The steroid hormone and glucocorticoid cortisol is the end-product of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and a key player in stress regulation (for reviews see e.g., Chrousos, 2009; Sapolsky, 2000a).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by review citations to Chrousos, 2009 and Sapolsky, 2000a

claim: Cortisol is considered an important mediator of the relation between chronic stress and stress-related disease.
source: Moreover, cortisol is considered an important mediator of the relation between chronic stress and stress-related disease (Adam et al., 2006; Miller et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adam et al., 2006 and Miller et al., 1995

claim: There is an association between hippocampal structural integrity and stress-related cortisol activity.
source: Previous research suggests an association between hippocampal structural integrity and stress-related cortisol activity (McEwen et al., 2016; McEwen, 1999), although findings are inconclusive.
evidence: Supported by citations to McEwen et al., 2016 and McEwen, 1999, though noted as inconclusive

claim: The hippocampus has a high glucocorticoid receptor density.
source: The hippocampus has a high glucocorticoid receptor density (Herman and Cullinan, 1997; Herman et al., 1995; Jacobson and Sapolsky, 1991; McEwen, 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Herman and Cullinan, 1997; Herman et al., 1995; Jacobson and Sapolsky, 1991; McEwen, 2013

claim: The hippocampal formation consists of multiple subfields including subiculum (SUB), cornu ammonis (CA1-3), and dentate gyrus (CA4/DG).
source: Having a three layered allocortex, the hippocampal formation consists of multiple subfields, or zones, starting at the subiculum (SUB) and moving inward to the hippocampus proper, the cornu ammonis (CA1-3), and dentate gyrus (CA4/DG) (Palomero-Gallagher et al., 2020; Wisse et al., 2017; Yushkevich et al., 2015; DeKraker et al., 2018).
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge supported by citations to Palomero-Gallagher et al., 2020; Wisse et al., 2017; Yushkevich et al., 2015; DeKraker et al., 2018

claim: Hippocampal subfields have unique microstructure.
source: These subfields have unique microstructure (Palomero-Gallagher et al., 2020; Wisse et al., 2017; Yushkevich et al., 2015; DeKraker et al., 2018; Paquola et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Palomero-Gallagher et al., 2020; Wisse et al., 2017; Yushkevich et al., 2015; DeKraker et al., 2018; Paquola et al., 2020

claim: Hippocampal subfields participate differently in the hippocampal circuitry.
source: These subfields have unique microstructure (Palomero-Gallagher et al., 2020; Wisse et al., 2017; Yushkevich et al., 2015; DeKraker et al., 2018; Paquola et al., 2020) and participate differently in the hippocampal circuitry (de Flores et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to de Flores et al., 2017

claim: Hippocampal subfields have different functional contributions.
source: participate differently in the hippocampal circuitry (de Flores et al., 2017), likely implicating different functional contributions (Hodgetts et al., 2017; Berron et al., 2016; Plachti et al., 2019; Genon et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2012; Vos de Wael et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hodgetts et al., 2017; Berron et al., 2016; Plachti et al., 2019; Genon et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2012; Vos de Wael et al., 2018

claim: Hippocampal subfields show functional correlation with a broad range of cortical regions, part of visual, control, and default functional networks.
source: Indeed, intrinsic functional MRI analyses have shown that the hippocampal subfields show functional correlation with a broad range of cortical regions, part of visual, control, and default functional networks (Paquola et al., 2020; Vos de Wael et al., 2018; Bayrak et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2019; Przeździk et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paquola et al., 2020; Vos de Wael et al., 2018; Bayrak et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2019; Przeździk et al., 2019

claim: Hippocampal subfield volumes and associated intrinsic functional connectivity are heritable.
source: Hippocampal subfield volumes and associated intrinsic functional connectivity have been shown to be heritable (Bayrak et al., 2022; Whelan et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bayrak et al., 2022 and Whelan et al., 2016

claim: Individual variation in hippocampal subfield structure and function is, in part, under genetic control.
source: Hippocampal subfield volumes and associated intrinsic functional connectivity have been shown to be heritable (Bayrak et al., 2022; Whelan et al., 2016), indicating that individual variation in subfield structure and function is, in part, under genetic control.
evidence: Inference from heritability findings cited from Bayrak et al., 2022 and Whelan et al., 2016

claim: Hippocampal structure and function are highly sensitive to contextual factors, such as stress.
source: Other lines of research have reported hippocampal structure and function to be highly sensitive to contextual factors, such as stress (McEwen, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to McEwen, 2013

claim: The hippocampus transmits negative feedback signals of glucocorticoid levels on HPA axis activity.
source: Mediated through its dense network of glucocorticoid receptors, the hippocampus transmits the negative feedback signals of a wide range of glucocorticoid levels on HPA axis activity (Jacobson and Sapolsky, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacobson and Sapolsky, 1991

claim: The hippocampus is linked to emotional reactivity through its inhibitory role on HPA axis dynamics.
source: Through this inhibitory role on HPA axis dynamics, it is linked to emotional reactivity (Phelps, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Phelps, 2004

claim: The hippocampus is linked to stress sensitivity through its inhibitory role on HPA axis dynamics.
source: Through this inhibitory role on HPA axis dynamics, it is linked to emotional reactivity (Phelps, 2004), stress sensitivity (McEwen, 1999; Bannerman et al., 2004; Franklin et al., 2012; Pruessner et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to McEwen, 1999; Bannerman et al., 2004; Franklin et al., 2012; Pruessner et al., 2010

claim: The hippocampus is causally involved in a variety of stress-related disorders.
source: Through this inhibitory role on HPA axis dynamics, it is linked to emotional reactivity (Phelps, 2004), stress sensitivity (McEwen, 1999; Bannerman et al., 2004; Franklin et al., 2012; Pruessner et al., 2010), and causally involved in a variety of stress-related disorders (O'Doherty et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Doherty et al., 2015

claim: A reduced cortisol awakening response has been associated with smaller hippocampal volume in healthy individuals.
source: Thus, a reduced cortisol awakening response, the response to the anticipated demands of the upcoming day (Fries et al., 2009), has been associated with smaller hippocampal volume in healthy individuals (Pruessner et al., 2007; Pruessner et al., 2005; Bruehl et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pruessner et al., 2007; Pruessner et al., 2005; Bruehl et al., 2009

claim: A reduced cortisol awakening response has been associated with smaller hippocampal volume in different psychiatric and metabolic conditions.
source: a reduced cortisol awakening response, the response to the anticipated demands of the upcoming day (Fries et al., 2009), has been associated with smaller hippocampal volume in healthy individuals (Pruessner et al., 2007; Pruessner et al., 2005; Bruehl et al., 2009) and different psychiatric (Dedovic et al., 2010; Dedovic et al., 2009) and metabolic (Bruehl et al., 2009; Ursache et al., 2012) conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dedovic et al., 2010; Dedovic et al., 2009 for psychiatric conditions and Bruehl et al., 2009; Ursache et al., 2012 for metabolic conditions

claim: Hippocampal integrity may be a necessary condition for the proper mounting of the cortisol awakening response.
source: In fact, the examination of patients with temporal lobe damage suggested that hippocampal integrity may be a necessary condition for the proper mounting of the CAR (Buchanan et al., 2004; Wolf et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buchanan et al., 2004 and Wolf et al., 2005

claim: Alterations in hippocampal functional connectivity have been reported to be associated with changes in cortisol levels.
source: Next, to changes in hippocampal structure, alterations in hippocampal functional connectivity have been reported to be associated with changes in cortisol levels (Hakamata et al., 2019; Chang and Yu, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hakamata et al., 2019 and Chang and Yu, 2019

claim: Elevated awakening, evening, diurnal, or 24 hour cortisol levels in healthy elderly are associated with age-related hippocampal atrophy.
source: There is also contrary work showing associations between elevated awakening, evening, diurnal, or 24 hour cortisol levels in healthy elderly with age-related hippocampal atrophy (Knoops et al., 2010; Lupien et al., 1999; Lupien et al., 1998; Sudheimer et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Knoops et al., 2010; Lupien et al., 1999; Lupien et al., 1998; Sudheimer et al., 2014

claim: Elevated cortisol levels are associated with hippocampal atrophy in samples with psychiatric conditions.
source: There is also contrary work showing associations between elevated awakening, evening, diurnal, or 24 hour cortisol levels in healthy elderly with age-related hippocampal atrophy (Knoops et al., 2010; Lupien et al., 1999; Lupien et al., 1998; Sudheimer et al., 2014) and, again, samples with psychiatric conditions (Gold et al., 2010; Mondelli et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gold et al., 2010 and Mondelli et al., 2010

claim: Mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) and compassion-focused therapy have gained in popularity as potential therapeutic tools to improve mental and physical health.
source: In recent years, contemplative mental training interventions, such as the mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) program (Kabat-Zinn, 1982) or compassion-focused therapy (Gilbert, 2014), have gained in popularity as potential therapeutic tools to improve mental and physical health (Goldberg et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kabat-Zinn, 1982; Gilbert, 2014; and Goldberg et al., 2018

claim: Mental training interventions can reduce stress.
source: In recent years, contemplative mental training interventions, such as the mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) program (Kabat-Zinn, 1982) or compassion-focused therapy (Gilbert, 2014), have gained in popularity as potential therapeutic tools to improve mental and physical health (Goldberg et al., 2018) and reducing stress (Khoury et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Khoury et al., 2015

claim: Mental training interventions can have a positive impact on the practitioner's stress sensitivity.
source: These mental training interventions can have a positive impact on the practitioner's stress sensitivity, making them a suitable model to investigate the interrelationship between training-related changes in hippocampal structure, function, and cortisol output.
evidence: General statement based on established research context

claim: Mindfulness-based interventions reduce reactive measures following acute psychosocial stress induction in the laboratory.
source: Next to reductions in reactive measures following acute psychosocial stress induction in the laboratory (Engert et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Engert et al., 2017

claim: Reduced subjective-psychological stress load is the most widely reported outcome of mental training interventions.
source: Next to reductions in reactive measures following acute psychosocial stress induction in the laboratory (Engert et al., 2017), reduced subjective-psychological stress load is the most widely reported outcome (for a review, see Khoury et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by review citation to Khoury et al., 2015

claim: Mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) reduces cortisol awakening response and afternoon/evening cortisol levels in healthy and diseased individuals.
source: Evidence for lower diurnal cortisol output stems mainly from mindfulness-based interventions, notably MBSR, for which reductions in CAR and afternoon/evening cortisol levels have been reported in healthy and diseased individuals (Brand et al., 2012; Carlson et al., 2007; Carlson et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brand et al., 2012; Carlson et al., 2007; Carlson et al., 2004

claim: Hair cortisol and cortisone are reduced through mental practice.
source: Moreover, other work in the current sample has shown that hair cortisol and cortisone are reduced through mental practice (Puhlmann et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Puhlmann et al., 2021b from the same study sample

claim: Hair cortisol measurements provide a window into long-term impact of cortisol exposure.
source: Hair cortisol measurements have been suggested to provide a window into long-term impact of cortisol exposure (Stalder et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stalder et al., 2017

claim: The ReSource Project investigated differential effects of distinct mental training practices on the association between changes in hippocampal subfields and diurnal cortisol profiles.
source: The current study, therefore, investigated differential effects of distinct mental training practices onto the association between changes in hippocampal subfields and underlying stress-related diurnal cortisol profiles changes in the context of a large-scale 9month mental training study, the ReSource Project (Singer et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement of the current study's aims with citation to Singer et al., 2016

claim: The ReSource Project included three 3-month Training Modules termed Presence, Affect, and Perspective.
source: Healthy participants attended three 3 months Training Modules termed Presence (cultivating attention and interoceptive awareness), Affect (cultivating compassion, prosocial motivation and dealing with difficult emotions) and Perspective (cultivating metacognition and perspective-taking on self and others) (Figure 1).
evidence: Description of study design with reference to Figure 1

claim: The Presence module cultivates attention and interoceptive awareness.
source: Healthy participants attended three 3 months Training Modules termed Presence (cultivating attention and interoceptive awareness)
evidence: Description of training module content

claim: The Affect module cultivates compassion, prosocial motivation and dealing with difficult emotions.
source: Affect (cultivating compassion, prosocial motivation and dealing with difficult emotions)
evidence: Description of training module content

claim: The Perspective module cultivates metacognition and perspective-taking on self and others.
source: Perspective (cultivating metacognition and perspective-taking on self and others)
evidence: Description of training module content

claim: The Presence module resembles typical mindfulness-based interventions but excludes socio-emotional or socio-cognitive practices.
source: Presence resembles typical mindfulness-based interventions, but excludes socio-emotional or socio-cognitive practices (Kabat-Zinn, 1982; Segal et al., 2002).
evidence: Description of training module with citations to Kabat-Zinn, 1982 and Segal et al., 2002

claim: The Affect module targets social skills through the training of socio-emotional and motivational skills such as empathy, compassion and care.
source: By contrast, Affect and Perspective target social skills through the training of either socio-emotional and motivational skills such as empathy, compassion and care (Affect)
evidence: Description of training module content

claim: The Perspective module targets social skills through the training of socio-cognitive skills such as perspective taking on self and others.
source: By contrast, Affect and Perspective target social skills through the training of either socio-emotional and motivational skills such as empathy, compassion and care (Affect) or socio-cognitive skills such as perspective taking on self and others (Perspective).
evidence: Description of training module content

claim: Training of socio-affective capacities specifically reduced cortisol awakening response.
source: In previous work, stemming from the same participant sample as examined here, we found a reduction in CAR specifically after the training of socio-affective capacities (Engert et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citation to Engert et al., 2023 from the same study sample

claim: Training of socio-affective or socio-cognitive capacities reduced acute stress reactivity.
source: In previous work, stemming from the same participant sample as examined here, we found a reduction in CAR specifically after the training of socio-affective capacities (Engert et al., 2023), and of acute stress reactivity after the training of socio-affective or socio-cognitive capacities (Engert et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Engert et al., 2017 from the same study sample

claim: Different types of mental practices equally reduced hair cortisol levels.
source: Alternatively, but also in the current sample, different types of mental practices equally reduced hair cortisol levels, a marker of long-term stress (Puhlmann et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Puhlmann et al., 2021b from the same study sample

claim: The content of mental training has a specific effect on daily cortisol changes but not on long-term stress levels.
source: This suggests that the content of mental training has a specific effect on daily cortisol changes but not on long-term stress levels.
evidence: Inference from previous findings in the same sample

claim: The three ReSource project Training Modules induced differentiable training-related changes in cortical structure and intrinsic functional organization.
source: Our group could also show differentiable training-related changes in cortical structure and intrinsic functional organization following the three ReSource project Training Modules, illustrating the existence of training-related structural plasticity of the social brain (Valk et al., 2017; Valk et al., 2023b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Valk et al., 2017 and Valk et al., 2023b from the same research group

claim: The study recruited 332 healthy adults (197 women, mean age 40.7±9.2 years, 20–55 years).
source: We recruited a total of 332 healthy adults (197 women, mean ± SD = 40.7±9.2 years, 20–55 years), in the winters of 2012/2013 and 2013/2014.
evidence: Description of study sample

claim: Participants were randomly assigned to two training cohorts (TC1, N=80; TC2, N=81).
source: In the Resource study, participants were randomly assigned to two training cohorts (TC1, N=80; TC2, N=81)
evidence: Description of study design

claim: TC1 and TC2 underwent a 9 months training consisting of three sequential Training Modules.
source: In the Resource study, participants were randomly assigned to two training cohorts (TC1, N=80; TC2, N=81) and underwent a 9 months training consisting of three sequential Training Modules (Presence, Affect, and Perspective)
evidence: Description of study design

claim: TC1 and TC2 started their training regimen with the Presence module and then underwent the latter two modules in different orders.
source: TC1 and TC2 started their training regimen with the Presence module, and then underwent the latter two modules in different orders (TC1: Affect-Perspective; TC2 Perspective-Affect) to serve as active control groups for each other (Figure 1C).
evidence: Description of study design with reference to Figure 1C

claim: TC3 completed three months of Affect training only.
source: Another active control group (TC3; N=81) completed three months of Affect training only.
evidence: Description of study design

claim: A matched test-retest control cohort (RCC, N=90) did not undergo any training.
source: Additionally, a matched test-retest control cohort did not undergo any training (RCC, N=90).
evidence: Description of study design

claim: All participants were examined at the end of each 3 months module (T1, T2, T3) using 3T MRI, behavioral and peripheral-physiological measures identical to baseline (T0) measures.
source: All participants were examined at the end of each 3 months module (T1, T2, T3) using 3T MRI, behavioral and peripheral-physiological measures that were identical to the baseline (T0) measures.
evidence: Description of study design and data collection

claim: Relative increases in right cornu ammonis 1–3 (CA1-3) were observed following Affect versus Perspective training.
source: We observed relative increases in right cornu ammonis 1–3 (CA1-3), but not in subiculum (SUB) or CA4 and dentate gyrus (CA4/DG) subfields, following Affect versus Perspective training (left: t=2.360, p=0.019, FDRq(q)>0.1, Cohens D=0.282; right: t=2.930, p=0.004, q=0.022, Cohens D=0.350)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of structural MRI data

claim: Bilateral CA1-3 volume showed subtle increases following Affect training.
source: that could be attributed to subtle increases (p<0.05) in bilateral CA1-3 volume following Affect (left: t=2.495, p=0.013, q=0.08, M: 25.511, std: 130.470, CI [–1.509 52.531]; right: t=2.374, p=0.018, q>0.1, M: 40.120, std: 181.300, CI [2.573 77.666])
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of structural MRI data

claim: Right CA1-3 volume showed subtle decreases following Perspective training.
source: and subtle decreases (p<0.05) in right CA1-3 volume following Perspective (left: t=−1.143, p>0.1, q>0.1, M:–23.048, std: 137.810, CI [–53.139 7.043]; right: t=−2.118, p=0.035, q>0.1, M:–39.602, std: 208.470, CI [–85.122 5.917]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of structural MRI data

claim: No differences were observed between Presence and the Active control cohort (Affect TC3).
source: We did not observe differences between Presence and the Active control cohort, Affect TC3.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of structural MRI data

claim: No overall change in hippocampal subfield volume was observed following mental training of nine months.
source: We observed no overall change in hippocampal subfield volume following mental training of nine months (Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of structural MRI data

claim: Accounting for intracranial volume (ICV) did not impact the main results regarding CA1-3 changes following Affect training.
source: Yet, accounting for ICV did not impact our main results, suggesting changes in CA1-3 following Affect were robust to sex differences in overall brain volume (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis controlling for ICV

claim: CA1-3 functional connectivity was strongest to medial prefrontal regions, precuneus extending to posterior cingulate, anterior temporal regions and angular gyrus at baseline.
source: Functional connectivity was strongest to medial prefrontal regions, precuneus extending to posterior cingulate, anterior temporal regions and angular gyrus (CA1-3: Figure 2; see Supplementary file 1 for other subfields).
evidence: Supported by functional MRI data analysis with reference to Figure 2

claim: The right CA1-3 functional network showed differential changes when comparing Affect training to Perspective training.
source: Evaluating functional connectivity changes, we found that the right CA1-3 functional network showed differential changes when comparing Affect training to Perspective training (2.420, p=0.016, q=0.032, Cohens D=0.289)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of functional MRI data

claim: Right CA1-3 mean functional connectivity showed subtle decreases following Perspective training.
source: which could be attributed to subtle (p<0.05) decreases in right CA1-3 mean FC following Perspective (t=−2.012, p=0.045, q>0.1, M:–0.024, std: 0.081, CI [-0.041–0.006])
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of functional MRI data

claim: Left CA1-3 connectivity showed decreases in connectivity to left posterior insula when comparing Affect to Perspective training.
source: Left CA1-3 connectivity showed decreases in connectivity to left posterior insula when comparing Affect to Perspective training (FDRq <0.05; t=−3.097, p=0.003, Cohens D=−0.370).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of functional MRI data

claim: Right CA1-3 showed connectivity increases to right mPFC when comparing Affect to Perspective training.
source: On the other hand, we observed connectivity increases between right CA1-3 to right mPFC for the same contrast (FDRq <0.05; t=3.262, p=0.002, Cohens D=0.389).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of functional MRI data

claim: Increases in bilateral CA1-3 following Affect showed a negative association with change in total diurnal cortisol output (AUCg).
source: We observed that increases in bilateral CA1-3 following Affect showed a negative association with change in total diurnal cortisol output (operationalized as the area under the curve with respect to ground; AUCg) (Table 5, left: t=–2.237, p=0.028, q=0.056; right: t=−2.283, p=0.025, q=0.05)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis correlating structural MRI changes with cortisol measures

claim: Reduction in stress-levels as measured by AUCg was associated with increases in CA1-3 volume.
source: indicating that with a reduction in stress-levels as measured by AUCg, there were increases in CA1-3 volume.
evidence: Interpretation of correlation between CA1-3 volume and AUCg

claim: Positive associations were observed between mean functional network of left CA1-3 and diurnal slope.
source: Yet, we observed positive associations between mean functional network of left CA1-3 and diurnal slope (t=2.653, p=0.01, q=0.02)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis correlating functional MRI changes with cortisol measures

claim: Positive associations were observed between mean functional network of left CA1-3 and AUCg.
source: Yet, we observed positive associations between mean functional network of left CA1-3 and diurnal slope (t=2.653, p=0.01, q=0.02) and AUCg (t=2.261, p=0.026, q=0.052)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis correlating functional MRI changes with cortisol measures

claim: AUCg modulated increases in connectivity between left CA1-3 and parietal occipital area.
source: When assessing whether particular regions within the CA1-3 network showed alterations in intrinsic functional connectivity, we observed that AUCg modulated increases in connectivity between left CA1-3 and parietal occipital area (q<0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of functional MRI data

claim: Consistent associations were identified between increases in LCA1-3 volume and intrinsic function and hair cortisol decreases.
source: We identified consistent associations between increases in LCA1-3 volume and intrinsic function and hair cortisol decreases (volume: t=−2.574, p=0.011, q=0.022, function: t=−2.700, p=0.008, q=0.016).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis correlating structural and functional MRI changes with hair cortisol measures

claim: Multivariate analysis identified significant associations between cortisol stress markers and hippocampal plasticity.
source: We found that both models could identify significant associations between cortisol stress markers and hippocampal plasticity (FDRq <0.05), and that in particular Affect showed strongest associations with the latent markers for CA1-3 (Table 7).
evidence: Supported by multivariate partial least squares analysis

claim: Both slope and AUC changes showed strongest associations with the latent factor in multivariate analysis.
source: Both analyses showed inverse effects of subfield structure and function in relation to stress markers and both slope and AUC changes showed strongest associations with the latent factor.
evidence: Supported by multivariate partial least squares analysis

claim: Compassion-based mental training alters CA1-3 structure.
source: Our longitudinal, multi-modal approach could thus show that compassion-based mental training alters CA1-3 structure.
evidence: Summary of findings from structural MRI analysis

claim: Training-based increases in CA1-3 volume related to decreases in total diurnal cortisol release.
source: Second, training-based increases in CA1-3 volume related to decreases in total diurnal cortisol release, suggesting that mental training and CA1-3 volume changes are linked to cortisol release.
evidence: Summary of findings from correlation analysis

claim: CA1-3 intrinsic functional change was associated with changes in diurnal cortisol slope and release, and long-term cortisol exposure.
source: Moreover, CA1-3 intrinsic functional change was associated with changes in diurnal cortisol slope and release, and long-term cortisol exposure.
evidence: Summary of findings from functional MRI correlation analysis

claim: The hippocampus is involved in the negative feedback inhibition of the HPA axis.
source: These results can be interpreted in line with the mainly inhibitory role of the hippocampus in stress regulation (Herman and Cullinan, 1997; Herman et al., 1995; Jacobson and Sapolsky, 1991; Herman et al., 2005). Specifically, the hippocampus is involved in the negative feedback inhibition of the HPA axis.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Herman and Cullinan, 1997; Herman et al., 1995; Jacobson and Sapolsky, 1991; Herman et al., 2005

claim: Mineral- and glucocorticoid receptors are present in abundance in hippocampal neurons.
source: Mineral- and glucocorticoid receptors are present in abundance in hippocampal neurons, from where they transmit the negative feedback signals of a wide range of glucocorticoid levels on HPA axis activity (Jacobson and Sapolsky, 1991).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation to Jacobson and Sapolsky, 1991

claim: The extremely high numbers of mineral- and glucocorticoid receptors make the hippocampus a prominent target for the neurotoxic effects of glucocorticoids.
source: The extremely high numbers of mineral- and glucocorticoid receptors make the hippocampus a prominent target for the neurotoxic effects of glucocorticoids (Sapolsky, 2000b; Sapolsky et al., 1985a; Sapolsky and Pulsinelli, 1985b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sapolsky, 2000b; Sapolsky et al., 1985a; Sapolsky and Pulsinelli, 1985b

claim: The CA1 may be susceptive to stress-based environmental effects due to synaptogenesis associated with NR2B subunits of glutamate receptors (NMDAR).
source: In particular the CA1 may be susceptive to stress-based environmental effects due to synaptogenesis associated with NR2B subunits of glutamate receptors (NMDAR) (Coultrap et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coultrap et al., 2005

claim: Sustained exposure to high glucocorticoid levels relates to calcium influx and may produce CA3 pyramidal neuronal damage in rodents and tree shrews.
source: Along these lines, sustained exposure to high glucocorticoid levels was shown to relate to calcium influx, and may produce CA3 pyramidal neuronal damage, which has been reported in rodents and tree shrews (McKittrick et al., 2000; Magariños et al., 1998; Magariños and McEwen, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to McKittrick et al., 2000; Magariños et al., 1998; Magariños and McEwen, 1995

claim: The mPFC plays a key role in HPA-axis regulation.
source: Accordingly, the mPFC, like the hippocampus, was shown to play a key role in HPA-axis regulation (Dedovic et al., 2009; Herman et al., 2005; Radley and Sawchenko, 2011; Diorio et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dedovic et al., 2009; Herman et al., 2005; Radley and Sawchenko, 2011; Diorio et al., 1993

claim: Glucose metabolism in the mPFC was negatively associated with acute stress-induced salivary cortisol increases.
source: In a previous positron emission tomography study, glucose metabolism in the mPFC was negatively associated with acute stress-induced salivary cortisol increases; notably, the authors observed a negative metabolic coupling between mPFC areas and the mesiotemporal lobe (Kern et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kern et al., 2008

claim: Structural changes in insular, opercular and orbitofrontal regions were observed following Affect training.
source: In related work on isocortical changes in structure and intrinsic function following the ReSource training, we have observed structural changes in insular, opercular and orbitofrontal regions following Affect training (Valk et al., 2017; Valk et al., 2023b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Valk et al., 2017 and Valk et al., 2023b from the same research group

claim: Both social modules (Affect and Perspective trainings) reduced acute cortisol reactivity to a psychosocial stressor.
source: For example, both social modules, that is the Affect and Perspective trainings, reduced acute cortisol reactivity to a psychosocial stressor (Kirschbaum et al., 1993), which is considered a dynamic state of HPA axis activity (Engert et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kirschbaum et al., 1993 and Engert et al., 2017

claim: Only Affect training was able to reduce the cortisol awakening response.
source: Regarding the CAR, only Affect training was able to reduce this dynamic cortisol response to awakening, known to reflect anticipatory stress (Engert et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Engert et al., 2023

claim: All Training Modules were equally effective in reducing hair cortisol over a training period of three to nine months.
source: Lastly, regarding hair cortisol, a long-term measure of systemic stress, all Training Modules were shown to be equally effective in stress reduction over a training period of three to nine months (Puhlmann et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Puhlmann et al., 2021b

claim: Non-adherence to saliva sampling in ambulatory settings exerts a significant impact on the resulting cortisol data.
source: It is of note that non-adherence to saliva sampling in ambulatory settings has been shown to exert a significant impact on the resulting cortisol data (Kudielka et al., 2007; Kudielka et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kudielka et al., 2007 and Kudielka et al., 2003

claim: The study did not employ objective measures for the verification of participants' sampling times.
source: Most importantly, we did not employ objective measures for the verification of participants' sampling times.
evidence: Statement of methodological limitation

claim: The study addressed the issue of non-adherence through an experience sampling approach based on mobile phones.
source: We nevertheless addressed the issue of non-adherence through an experience sampling approach based on mobile phones handed out to our participants.
evidence: Description of methodological approach

claim: The 3 months Affect training module cultivating compassion and care related to an increase of hippocampal CA1-3 subfield volume.
source: We find that only the 3 months Affect training module cultivating compassion and care, rather than attention-based (Presence) or socio-cognitive (Perspective) training, related to an increase of hippocampal CA1-3 subfield volume, with corresponding alterations in functional connectivity and a reduction in total diurnal cortisol output.
evidence: Summary of main findings from the study

claim: The Affect training module related to corresponding alterations in functional connectivity.
source: We find that only the 3 months Affect training module cultivating compassion and care, rather than attention-based (Presence) or socio-cognitive (Perspective) training, related to an increase of hippocampal CA1-3 subfield volume, with corresponding alterations in functional connectivity and a reduction in total diurnal cortisol output.
evidence: Summary of main findings from the study

claim: The Affect training module related to a reduction in total diurnal cortisol output.
source: We find that only the 3 months Affect training module cultivating compassion and care, rather than attention-based (Presence) or socio-cognitive (Perspective) training, related to an increase of hippocampal CA1-3 subfield volume, with corresponding alterations in functional connectivity and a reduction in total diurnal cortisol output.
evidence: Summary of main findings from the study

claim: Consistent alterations were observed between cortisol change and CA1-3 volume and function across analyses.
source: Across analyses we observed consistent alterations between cortisol change and CA1-3 volume and function, pinpointing this region as a potential target for further investigations on stress and the human brain.
evidence: Summary of findings across multiple analyses

claim: Multivariate analyses point to a circuit level understanding of latent diurnal stress scores.
source: Lastly, our multivariate analyses also point to a circuit level understanding of latent diurnal stress scores.
evidence: Summary of multivariate analysis findings

claim: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Magnetom Verio using a 32-channel head coil.
source: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Magnetom Verio (Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) using a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: Description of MRI acquisition parameters

claim: Hippocampal subfields (SUB, CA1-3, and CA4/DG) were segmented using a patch-based algorithm.
source: Based on the available high-resolution T1-weighted images subiculum (SUB), CA1-3, and CA4/DG were segmented using a patch-based algorithm in all participants individually (see further Caldairou et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of segmentation method with citation to Caldairou et al., 2016

claim: The patch-based algorithm has shown high segmentation accuracy of hippocampal subfields.
source: In previous validations work, this algorithm has shown high segmentation accuracy of hippocampal subfields (Caldairou et al., 2016), and in detecting hippocampal subfield pathology in patients with epilepsy (Bernhardt et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caldairou et al., 2016 and Bernhardt et al., 2016

claim: 14 saliva samples (7 per day) were obtained over the course of two consecutive weekdays for cortisol assessment.
source: For cortisol assessment, 14 saliva samples (7 per day) were obtained over the course of two consecutive weekdays (Mondays/Tuesdays, Wednesdays/Thursdays or Thursdays/Fridays, depending on participant availability).
evidence: Description of cortisol sampling protocol

claim: Samples were taken upon free awakening and at 30 min, 60 min, 4, 6, 8, and 10 hr after awakening.
source: In detail, samples were taken upon free awakening (while still in bed; S1) and at 30 min, 60 min, 4, 6, 8, and 10 hr after awakening.
evidence: Description of cortisol sampling protocol

claim: Cortisol levels were determined using a time-resolved fluorescence immunoassay.
source: Cortisol levels (expressed in nmol/l) were determined using a time-resolved fluorescence immunoassay (Dressendörfer et al., 1992) with intra-/inter-assay variability of 10/12%.
evidence: Description of cortisol assay method with citation to Dressendörfer et al., 1992

claim: Hair samples were taken as close as possible to the scalp from a posterior vertex position at T0 and after each following timepoint (T0-T3).
source: To evaluate cortisol and cortisone, hair strands were taken as close as possible to the scalp from a posterior vertex position at T0 and after each following timepoint (T0-T3).
evidence: Description of hair cortisol sampling protocol

claim: The proximal 3 cm segment of hair was evaluated to study accumulation of cortisol and cortisone over each 3-month period.
source: We evaluated the proximal 3 cm segment of hair to study accumulation of cortisol and cortisone over each 3-month period, based on the assumption of an average hair growth rate of 1 cm/month (Wennig, 2000).
evidence: Description of hair cortisol analysis method with citation to Wennig, 2000

claim: Hormone concentrations were captured using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry.
source: Hormone concentrations were captured using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry, the current criterion standard approach for hair steroid analysis (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of assay method with citation to Gao et al., 2016
